statement: Six people are in a room. Each is either a truth-teller, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Every one of them says: "More than half of the other five people in this room are liars." How many liars are in the room?

choices.misconception: I assumed that six people all saying the same thing must all be telling the truth.
I thought more than half of all six people had to be liars, so I took the smallest such number, 4.
I assumed, as in other liar puzzles, that exactly one person could be telling the truth.
I assumed that six people all saying the same thing must all be lying.

hints: Each speaker talks about the other five. Nobody counts themselves.
Suppose there are L liars. A truth-teller sees L liars among the others, but a liar sees only L - 1. Write what each type's statement forces, then check the cases where everyone is the same type.
A truth-teller needs L to be at least 3, and a liar needs L - 1 to be at most 2.

solutions.reliable: Let L be the number of liars. A truth-teller's claim is true, so the L liars among the other five number at least 3, which means L is at least 3. A liar's claim is false, so the L - 1 liars among the other five number at most 2, which means L is at most 3. If both types are present, both conditions hold, so L = 3. Check the extremes: with no liars at all, each truth-teller would be claiming at least 3 liars among the others when there are none, a contradiction. With six liars, each sees 5 liars among the others, so their claim would be true, also a contradiction. So there are 3 liars: each truth-teller sees 3 liars among the others, and each liar sees only 2. The transferable idea: when everyone makes the same statement, the speaker's own type changes what they see, so write a separate condition for each type.

whyOnTest: Identical statements from both types force you to account for each speaker leaving themselves out, a 5-point idea that trips anyone who reasons by symmetry.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
